meta.rule: Energy generated only; no installed capacity or consumption data used for forecasting or comparison.

balanced.label: Government plan (CEA 2030)
balanced.note: Solar and wind follow S-curves fitted to FY2019-26 generation shares and meet CEA's 2029-30 generation plan (thermal 56%, nuclear 3.8%, hydro 9.1%, other renewables 31%) in FY2030. After 2030 the S-curves continue to ceilings of 40% solar and 14% wind. Nuclear reaches 8% and hydro eases to 7.5% by 2047 (assumptions: the nuclear and hydro goals are stated in GW, which this model does not use).

accelerated.label: Accelerated clean
accelerated.note: Same 2030 anchor as the government plan, then higher ceilings (50% solar, 18% wind) and nuclear at 11% by 2047. Needs large storage and inter-regional transmission.

trend.label: Current trends
trend.note: Solar and wind S-curves fitted to FY2019-26 only, with no government anchor (ceilings 40% and 14%); nuclear, hydro and gas keep their recent trend. Falls short of CEA's 2030 generation plan.

North.role: Solar powerhouse with Himalayan hydro for firming
strengths: Highest solar resource: Rajasthan's Thar desert and Ladakh hold ~45% of India's assessed solar potential, with the best irradiance in the country
Himalayan rivers in Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand and J&K: about a third of the large-hydro potential
Wind along western Rajasthan; nuclear at Rawatbhata, Mahi Banswara and Gorakhpur
actions: Grow solar fastest here and ship daytime surplus over the Green Energy Corridors
Use reservoir hydro and pumped storage in the hills to shift solar into evening peaks
No new coal: the region has almost no coal reserves, so new thermal would rely on long-haul coal
North.policy: National Solar Mission, Green Energy Corridor (Phase I-II), Ladakh renewable transmission project

West.role: Balanced hub: wind-solar parks, pit-head coal and nuclear
strengths: Gujarat and Maharashtra together hold over a third of India's 120 m wind potential
Chhattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh coal fields (about 30% of coal resources) support pit-head plants
Nuclear sites at Tarapur, Kakrapar, Chutka and Jaitapur; Gujarat's Khavda renewable park
actions: Pair Gujarat-Rajasthan wind and solar with storage; build hybrid parks on desert and salt-pan land
Keep coal growth at pit-heads in Chhattisgarh/MP and retire old far-from-mine units first
Bring the approved nuclear projects online for firm low-carbon output
West.policy: Wind-Solar Hybrid Policy, offshore wind roadmap (Gujarat coast), Nuclear Energy Mission

strengths: Best wind belt: Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh hold ~43% of 120 m wind potential
Strong solar in the Deccan plateau (AP, Karnataka, Telangana)
Kudankulam, Kalpakkam, Kaiga and the planned Kovvada site; offshore wind off Tamil Nadu
actions: Repower old Tamil Nadu turbines and add offshore wind in the Gulf of Mannar
Expand nuclear at existing coastal sites (cooling water, approved land)
Use Western Ghats pumped storage to balance the monsoon wind peak
South.policy: National Repowering Policy for wind, offshore wind bidding trajectory, Nuclear Energy Mission

strengths: Jharkhand, Odisha and West Bengal hold over half of India's coal resources
Teesta (Sikkim) and Odisha rivers for hydro and pumped storage
Weaker sun and wind than the west and south
actions: Run the most efficient pit-head supercritical coal plants here as the country's firm backup
Plan for the region to import clean power as coal's share falls; build the eastern-western links
Re-use coal-mine land for solar and pumped storage; a just-transition plan for mining districts
East.policy: Coal-to-clean transition plans, pit-head siting guidelines, Green Energy Corridor (inter-state)

strengths: Arunachal Pradesh alone holds ~40% of India's large-hydro potential (Brahmaputra basin)
Natural gas in Assam and Tripura
actions: Develop storage hydro on the Brahmaputra tributaries in stages, with basin-level environmental and seismic review
Export firm hydro over the North-East-to-North/West HVDC links
Keep gas for peaking; add rooftop and small solar for local supply
North-East.policy: Hydro policy (renewable status for large hydro, 2019), NE region power master plan, HVDC corridors

mix_model.method: Logistic S-curves for solar and wind fitted on FY2019-26 generation shares; ceilings are assumptions; nuclear, hydro, gas and bio-waste follow anchored linear paths; coal is the remainder.
mix_model.goals_used: CEA Optimal Generation Capacity Mix 2029-30 (V2.0, 2023): generation shares thermal 55.9%, nuclear 3.8%, hydro 9.1%, other renewables 31.2%.
mix_model.goals_not_used: Capacity targets (500 GW non-fossil by 2030, 100 GW nuclear and 1,800 GW non-fossil by 2047) are installed-capacity measures and are excluded by the challenge rule.

viksit.label: Viksit Bharat ($30 trillion)
viksit.note: steady real growth that makes GDP $30 trillion in 2047 (Rs 7,365 lakh crore at Rs 246 per dollar: today's Rs 92.65 falling 4.75% a year)

wb.label: World Bank high-income path
wb.note: 7.8% real growth a year, the average the World Bank says India needs to reach high income by 2047

imf.label: IMF outlook
imf.note: IMF medium-term potential growth of 6.5% to 2030, easing to 5.5% by 2047

dataset.label: Dataset trend
dataset.note: the dataset's own 2014-2024 GSDP growth, held flat

states.note: State production need = region need split by the generation equation with state population, GSDP per person and urban share (from each state's FY2025-26 generation). Proposed production = state's FY2025-26 generation plus its share of the region's growth in each source: waste-to-energy by 2047 urban population (capped at 45% of a region), other sources by 5-year average generation.
